ig_carousel_topic.topic: Hedging: when it's smart, when it's just buying back losses
ig_carousel_topic.slide1_text: Hedging a bet feels smart. Sometimes it is. Most of the time you're just paying to feel better.
ig_carousel_topic.slide2_text: The misconception: hedging always reduces risk. What bettors actually do is lock in a small win the moment a big one feels close. That's not risk management, that's fear management.
ig_carousel_topic.slide3_text: Real hedging has one job: locking in guaranteed profit when the math works out. If your original bet is still -EV at current prices, hedging a loser just turns one loss into two smaller ones.
ig_carousel_topic.slide4_text: Example: you bet Team A ML at +200 ($50 to win $100). They're up big in the 4th. Team A is now -350 live. To guarantee $40 profit either way, you'd need to lay $140 on the other side. That $140 risk for $40 upside is usually a bad trade.
ig_carousel_topic.slide5_text: Hedge only when the guaranteed profit is worth the stake you're giving up. If you're hedging because you're nervous, that's not strategy. That's your bankroll paying for your anxiety.
ig_carousel_topic.caption: Hedging feels like discipline. Usually it's just fear. Swipe to see when the math actually supports it and when you're just buying back a loss.
